templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Emphasis: stronger same-direction fact (content-contrast trap at hard)
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Japanese architect Hajime Narukawa’s AuthaGraph world map is praised for showing the relative sizes of landmasses and oceans more accurately than the familiar Mercator projection. ______ no flat map can represent a globe’s curved surface without some distortion. Even so, by dividing the sphere into 96 triangles and unfolding them into a rectangle, Narukawa keeps that distortion unusually small.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence praises the AuthaGraph map for its accuracy. The blank sentence concedes an obvious point that seems to cut against that praise: every flat map distorts a globe somewhat. The next sentence turns back with “Even so” to show how Narukawa keeps the distortion small. “Of course” marks this concession of a well-known fact before the turn.

A.why_wrong: The map’s accuracy is not the reason flat maps distort a globe; the sentence concedes a general limit that the next sentence answers.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does not reword the praise in the first sentence; it grants a point that cuts against it.

D.why_wrong: That every flat map distorts a globe is not a further point in the map’s favor; it is a concession, which is why the next sentence opens with “Even so.”

items.notes: Grant then turn, the turn opened by Even so in the next sentence (3.19 shape; b1 used But, b2 though, w1 Still, Yet and but). K1 has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5): written as a strong band 6. Key Of course because the point conceded is common knowledge (every flat map distorts), the lesson from b1 and b2 (Granted for new information). No contrast decoy (excluded beside a concession key) and no In fact or Indeed (second-sense rule). Additionally dies on the next sentence's Even so as well as on content. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no invented names and no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

notes: Attribution rule applied (Transitions, no fact-checking): no made-up finding attributed to a real named person or organisation; Narukawa's AuthaGraph (96 triangles unfolded to a rectangle) is his real work

items.passage: In films and novels, medieval books are nearly always copied by monks in candlelit monasteries. Historians who have examined tax rolls and university records from thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Paris, however, paint a different picture; ______ they have found, books there were made not by monks but by lay scribes, illuminators, and binders who worked for pay in the city’s shops.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the familiar image of monks copying books, and the clause before the blank says that historians who studied Paris records paint a different picture. The clause after the blank supplies that picture: in Paris, books were usually made by paid lay artisans rather than by monks. “More often” fits because the clause gives the more common case that the records reveal, without denying that monks copied some books.

A.why_wrong: The clause does not hold true in spite of the historians’ different picture; it is that picture, so nothing is being conceded.

B.why_wrong: The historians’ findings do not cause books to have been made by lay artisans; the clause states what the records show.

C.why_wrong: The clause is not a further point added to the historians’ different picture; it spells out what that picture is.

items.notes: Band-7 S1 on the d3b7d7a3 frame (the only band-7 S1 model; the reviewers kept the restatement and specification forms at band 6): a familiar picture, a however clause saying the evidence differs, then after a semicolon and the interrupter they have found the common case, keyed more often. Varied from w1b1_03 (in many cases, radar) and w1b3_02 (sentence-initial More often after a figure): no share or number, the popular picture comes from films and novels rather than a narrative or image formula, and the clause before the blank is paint a different picture, not complicates. Decoys checked against both clauses: nonetheless would set the lay workshops against the historians' picture, which they are; consequently would make the records the cause; in addition would leave a different picture empty. Register 5.12 chars/word misses band-7 gate 4 (5.3), but proxy 3 passes: however in sentence 2, not by monks but in B, one adversative decoy. Escalation reading avoided (the clause before the blank and the interrupter are the same historians at the same strength, so in addition cannot read as suggest then prove). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no invented names and no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

surface contrast: B says not by monks but by lay artisans right after a however clause, so nonetheless pulls on a first read
in addition pulls because B, introduced by they have found, can look like a second finding beside the different picture; consequently pulls because the findings seem to lead to the clause

items.passage: British composer Cornelius Cardew came to believe that making music should not be restricted to professionals with years of training. ______ in Paragraph 7 of his choral work The Great Learning, he abandoned standard notation in favor of brief written instructions. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence states Cardew’s aim: performing music should be open to people without formal training. The blank sentence describes a choice he made in service of that aim, replacing notation that takes training to read with brief instructions, which the last sentence shows any singer can follow. “To that end” signals an action taken to achieve the goal just stated.

B.why_wrong: The sentence does not restate Cardew’s belief; it describes a specific decision he made in one composition.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does not describe a second case like the first; it describes a step Cardew took because of his belief.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in Cardew’s belief would make simple rules for untrained singers unexpected; the choice follows the belief rather than defying it.

items.explanation: The first sentence describes how the book looks on the surface: a set of exact descriptions of animals. The blank sentence gives what the book is about in the end, human beings, whom Arreola sees reflected in each creature. “Ultimately” signals this final, deeper meaning behind the surface.

B.why_wrong: The sentence does not add one more feature to the animal descriptions; it says what the book is really about, which is why it speaks of a “true subject.”

D.why_wrong: The sentence is not one instance of the animal descriptions; it states the book’s underlying subject.

A.why_wrong: The conclusion does not hold in spite of Triton’s backward orbit; it follows from it.

B.why_wrong: The conclusion is not a case like Triton’s orbit; it is drawn from that orbit.

C.why_wrong: The astronomers’ conclusion is not an example of the rule in the first sentence; it is an inference from Triton breaking that rule.
